page: Vultr voc-m-4c-32gb-400s-amd belongs to the Optimized Cloud Compute family, engineered primarily for memory-optimized workloads requiring a generous RAM-to-core ratio. The server is configured with 4 dedicated x86_64 vCPUs mapped across 2 physical cores on an AMD EPYC processor running at a base clock of 2.0 GHz. System memory totals 32.0 GB, yielding 8.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. The instance includes 400 GB of local NVMe SSD storage and provides one complimentary public IPv4 address. There are no discrete hardware accelerators or GPUs provisioned on this configuration. Supported CPU vector and cryptographic instructions include AVX-512, VNNI, AES, and SHA-NI.

Performance benchmarks show notable strength in single-threaded operations and memory subsystem write throughput. In single-core stress-ng tests, the machine achieves top-tier results, complemented by strong Geekbench single-core, text processing, and gzip compression measurements. Uncached large-block memory writes also demonstrate strong throughput at 112.99 GB/sec. However, multi-threaded operations reflect the underlying hardware constraint of two physical cores, registering average scores across multi-core Geekbench and compilation tests, and bottom-quartile throughput in multi-threaded bzip3 decompression and static web serving. Evaluated database operations and medium-sized LLM prompt processing similarly fall into lower performance tiers.

Given its hardware topology, Vultr voc-m-4c-32gb-400s-amd offers qualitative resource efficiency for memory-bound tasks that do not demand extensive parallel compute. Workloads that benefit from local NVMe storage and large RAM footprints, such as in-memory key-value stores like Redis, intermediate data transformation pipelines, and text analysis services, match its technical strengths effectively.
description: Vultr voc-m-4c-32gb-400s-amd is a memory-optimized virtual machine within the Optimized Cloud Compute family. It features 4 dedicated x86_64 vCPUs derived from 2 physical cores on an AMD EPYC processor clocked at 2.0 GHz, alongside 32 GB of system RAM and a bundled 400 GB NVMe SSD. Operating without GPU hardware, the instance provides an 8 GB per vCPU ratio, making it well balanced for memory-intensive environments. In benchmark testing, the platform shows strong single-core execution, placing in the top tiers for single-thread stress-ng and Geekbench evaluations, alongside high-bandwidth memory write operations. Conversely, multi-core throughput and raw database transactions sit in average to lower performance tiers, reflecting the physical two-core constraint. From a cost-efficiency perspective, the high memory allocation per vCPU makes it cost effective for workloads bound by memory footprints rather than heavy multi-threaded execution, such as in-memory caches, data transformation, and text analysis services.
